body.text: From Metula on the Lebanese border to Eilat on the Red Sea, Israelis remained glued to their television screens on the night of November 3-4. Midterm elections were taking place thousands of kilometres away in the US, but they carried implications for the survival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

A week earlier, Arab-Israeli voters had delivered an electoral blow to Netanyahu, depriving his right-wing coalition of a parliamentary majority. But the veteran politician was not ready to surrender power. His hopes of remaining Prime Minister rested partly on his close relationship with US President Donald Trump, who had been encouraging the formation of a broader Israeli government by drawing right-wing constituents from the opposition alliance into an arrangement with Netanyahu. The US midterm results threatened to upset those calculations.

Netanyahu’s coalition emerged from the October 27 Knesset elections with only 53 seats (against 68 in the last election) in Israel’s 120-member parliament, where a majority requires 61 seats. The Jewish-led opposition, headed by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, secured 48 seats. Of the 2 Palestinian-led formations, the Joint List secured 11 seats, while Ra’am won 8. Their combined 19 seats represents a historic achievement for Palestinian-led parties.

Together, the parties opposed to Netanyahu got 67 seats. But the arithmetic concealed a political obstacle: several Jewish opposition leaders remained unwilling to form a government dependent on Palestinian representatives. Netanyahu hoped to exploit that division.

The possibility of a national unity government, bringing Eisenkot or other right-wing opposition leaders into an administration headed by Netanyahu, offered one route to preserving his premiership. It would also keep Palestinian parties outside the governing arrangement.

Trump’s support was considered potentially important in such an exercise. His administration’s regional priorities, particularly confrontation with Iran and maintaining Israeli military cooperation with the US, could be invoked to justify a broad emergency government. But the proposed arrangement encountered resistance as the Americans voted in midterm elections.

After the Democratic sweep of the US Congress, Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid said that the midterm election results had eliminated any remaining prospect of a national unity government headed by Netanyahu. “Israel cannot afford for him [Netanyahu] to remain prime minister. It endangers security, it endangers democracy, it will crush us in the world,” Lapid wrote on X. “The American election results in the morning have one unexpected outcome: they eliminate any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu,” he added.

Yair Golan, leader of The Democrats party, warned that Netanyahu’s continued rule could push an already isolated Israel further towards “international sanctions, international isolation and a collision with the United States”. Eisenkot also rejected suggestions to join a Netanyahu-led government, indicating that even a personal appeal from Trump would not change his position. Other opposition politicians argued that Netanyahu’s close identification with Trump had compromised Israel’s ability to maintain bipartisan relationships in the US.

The US midterm results did not deprive Trump of his presidential authority or eliminate US support for Israel. But they created a Congress with greater capacity to scrutinise the administration’s foreign policy and challenge its decisions.

The situation became more complicated when Trump announced, on November 3, plans to end direct US military assistance to Israel by the end of 2026. The announcement raised questions about the existing $38-billion, 10-year assistance framework, which runs through 2028. Ending assistance before that agreement expires would involve legal and congressional considerations, and the announcement did not itself terminate the programme.
Israel’s President intervenes

On November 4, as Israelis absorbed the US midterm results, President Isaac Herzog formally received the certified results of their own parliamentary election. The ceremony produced an unusually pointed intervention with Herzog condemning racist rhetoric directed against Israel’s Arab community following the election, during which Netanyahu’s supporters had alleged fraud and foreign interference involving Palestinian voters. “I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” Herzog declared.

The President also expressed confidence in the security and law enforcement agencies investigating allegations of foreign interference. His intervention followed the Central Elections Committee’s rejection of claims that widespread fraud had affected the results. A separate investigation into suspected foreign interference remained open, but election officials said it did not invalidate the outcome.

Herzog’s remarks were significant because Netanyahu and his allies attempted to cast suspicion on the exceptional participation of Palestinian citizens. The President effectively reminded Israel’s political establishment that the votes of Arab citizens could not be treated as less legitimate than those of Jewish citizens. He also acknowledged the absence of a clear governing majority and called on political parties to compromise rather than force the country into another election.

On November 3, leaders of the principal Jewish-led opposition parties met in Herzliya and agreed to support Eisenkot’s effort to replace Netanyahu. They announced their intention to work towards a national emergency government. The meeting represented a significant development after several days of disagreements over how to translate the election result into a change of government.

Yet one question remained unresolved. Could the opposition form a government without the 19 Palestinian lawmakers? The Joint List of Arab parties offered to support an alternative government from outside the coalition. Islamic Ra’am, which had previously participated in an Israeli governing coalition, was also open to cooperation.

The central contradiction of Israel’s election was becoming impossible to avoid. Netanyahu had lost his majority because Palestinian citizens voted in unprecedented numbers. But the politicians seeking to replace him were struggling to accept those same voters as legitimate participants in determining the next government.

The overall voter turnout was 77.9 per cent, the highest in decades. Palestinian participation was estimated at nearly 80 per cent, a dramatic increase from the approximately 38 per cent recorded in 2022.
The Arab priorities

In Rahat, the largest Bedouin city in Israel’s southern Negev desert, a 56-year-old Palestinian woman walked into a polling station to vote in an Israeli parliamentary election for the first time. Dressed in black, with only her eyes visible, she declined to give her name or be photographed. But she captured the anger sweeping through Palestinian communities. “The government’s behaviour had hurt our souls,” she said.

Her family lived in an unrecognised Bedouin village without electricity or running water. Building even a modest shelter could invite demolition. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir wanted to demolish everything.

Across the Negev, women who had rarely participated in national elections joined queues outside polling stations. Images and accounts of Bedouin voters arriving on camels, horses, and donkeys circulated during the election. For communities living in remote desert settlements, voting could itself require a considerable journey.

In some Palestinian localities, voters complained of intimidation, police intervention, and delays at polling stations. The legal rights organisation Adalah reported unusually slow identity checks and questioning of voters.

Nimr Abu Shiban, a resident of Rahat, told The Times of Israel that his wife and daughters would not ordinarily have voted. “But the country is in such bad hands that everyone is voting today,” he said.
The turnout drew a reaction from Netanyahu.

In most democracies, a political leader would welcome the participation of a previously disengaged section of the electorate. Netanyahu treated the mobilisation of Palestinian citizens, who constitute roughly one-fifth of Israel’s population, as an emergency. He urged Jewish supporters to rush to polling stations. Images of Bedouin voters were used to warn that Palestinian participation threatened the Right. Clearly, the Prime Minister was alarmed that a substantial section of the population was exercising its democratic rights.

The Israeli journalist Meron Rapoport summed up the electoral verdict: Netanyahu had lost, but he had not been defeated. Although his coalition had suffered a substantial setback, his opponents had failed to secure a governing majority without Palestinian support.

For years, Israel’s Jewish opposition parties had calculated that they could defeat Netanyahu without depending on Palestinian votes. They believed a combination of military credentials, nationalist appeals and opposition to ultra-orthodox political influence would be sufficient. The October election demonstrated the limits of that strategy. Without the exceptional Palestinian turnout, Netanyahu’s coalition might have retained its majority.
Ahmad Tibi: We can help remove Netanyahu

In a conversation with this writer, Ahmad Tibi, a veteran Palestinian politician belonging to the Joint List, urged the opposition to move swiftly and establish a government headed by Eisenkot rather than allow Netanyahu to exploit divisions among his opponents.

Tibi said that the Joint List does not seek to be included in the government but is prepared to provide outside support to a governing coalition that may not include Palestinian parties. “We have spoken about providing a safety net for our community and making it possible to bring down Netanyahu’s government and establish an alternative government through understandings with the opposition,” he said.

Such an arrangement would resemble the parliamentary support that Arab lawmakers provided to Yitzhak Rabin’s government in the 1990s. Tibi stressed that Palestinian representatives would seek commitments addressing the needs of their communities in exchange for their support. “The most important thing for us now is to bring down this government,” he added.

He described the extraordinary Palestinian turnout as a political achievement that had disrupted Netanyahu’s plans of forming “another government under his leadership”. He also accused Netanyahu’s supporters of attempting to delegitimise Palestinian voters through allegations of electoral fraud. He was confident that the election result would prevent Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich (Netanyahu’s Finance Minister) from returning to ministerial office. Tibi was also open to coordinating with Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, despite the differences between the two Palestinian political formations.

Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen confirmed that preliminary contact had been made with several opposition figures, including Eisenkot, Yair Golan, and members of Bennett’s party, but no formal agreement had emerged. Besides, Avigdor Liberman, who leads Yisrael Beytenu party, remained opposed to relying on Arab support.
Unwanted kingmakers

For readers unfamiliar with Israeli politics, the Palestinian electoral formations require some explanation. The Joint List is an alliance of three distinct political organisations: Hadash, Ta’al and Balad. Hadash is a left-wing formation rooted in communist and socialist politics. It includes Jewish and Palestinian members and emphasises equality, workers’ rights, and opposition to occupation. Ta’al, associated with Tibi, concentrates on the political and civil rights of Palestinian citizens of Israel. Balad takes a more explicitly Palestinian nationalist position, advocating the transformation of Israel into a state of equal citizenship rather than one that gives constitutional preference to Jewish national identity. It also stresses Palestinian collective rights and has historically resisted participation in Zionist-led governments.

Ra’am, the United Arab List, emerged from the southern branch of Israel’s Islamic Movement and combines socially conservative roots with pragmatic parliamentary politics. Its leader, Mansour Abbas, argues that Palestinian citizens cannot wait indefinitely for a comprehensive peace settlement before demanding improvements in schools, housing, municipal budgets, and public security.

In 2021, Ra’am became the first independent Arab-majority party to join an Israeli ruling coalition, entering the administration led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. In 2026, Abbas moved the party further towards an independent civic political identity by separating its decision-making from the Islamic Movement’s Shura Council.

The two Palestinian formations disagree over the extent to which they should participate directly in Israeli governments. But both recognise that their combined parliamentary strength could determine who becomes Prime Minister.

Jabareen has identified four conditions for supporting a government that replaces Netanyahu: action against organised crime, development and expansion of Palestinian communities, equal civil rights, and a clear political process towards an independent Palestinian state. The final demand connects the immediate grievances of Palestinian citizens inside Israel to the unresolved question of Palestinian self-determination.
For Eisenkot and his prospective allies, this presents a difficult choice.
Racism behind the deadlock

Sami Abou Shahadeh, a prominent Palestinian politician associated with Balad, had told this writer in an earlier interview that that the parliamentary arithmetic should have been straightforward: Netanyahu’s bloc had lost its majority, while parties opposing his continued rule collectively held enough seats to form a government. “But because of the racism within Israeli society, we are still debating whether or not this was a decisive outcome.”
Speaking of Eisenkot’s Moroccan Jewish ancestry, he said: “Eisenkot, a leader of Arab, specifically Moroccan, descent, says he refuses to sit with Arabs. This is a racist society.”

His remarks reflected a larger frustration. Palestinian citizens were encouraged to participate in the elections, but their elected representatives are considered politically unacceptable by much of the Jewish establishment.

The anger driving Palestinian participation was not confined to the war in Gaza. Across Galilee, from Nazareth and Sakhnin to Tamra and Shefa-Amr, Palestinian citizens confront inequalities often obscured by Israel’s image as a prosperous high-tech economy. In contrast to affluent Jewish neighbourhoods, nearby Arab localities struggle with inadequate infrastructure, overcrowded housing, and limited municipal resources.

According to the Israel Democracy Institute’s 2024 statistical report, 95 per cent of Arab localities fell within the four lowest categories of Israel’s 10-category socio-economic ranking. In 2023, 38.4 per cent of Arab families lived below the poverty line. Organised crime has compounded these inequalities. The Abraham Initiatives recorded 252 Arab citizens killed in circumstances related to crime and violence in 2025.

The political commentator Tal Schneider rejected the suggestion that the violence reflected some inherent characteristic of Arab society, pointing instead to weak policing, poverty, and years of inadequate investment. She described the gap between Jewish and Arab society as appalling.

For Bedouin communities in the Negev, the immediate concern was the threat of demolition and the absence of basic services. In northern towns, the priorities included housing, employment, municipal resources, and protection from organised crime.

For many others, the war in Gaza and the continuing occupation of Palestinian territories gave the election a significance extending beyond their immediate circumstances. For decades, Palestinians holding Israeli citizenship had debated whether participation in Knesset elections legitimised a state that constitutionally privileges Jewish national identity. Some boycotted elections on principle. Others considered participation necessary to defend their communities against increasingly hostile governments.

This time, many appeared to conclude that abstention would only strengthen Netanyahu’’s coalition with Ben-Gvir and Smotrich. Participation in an electoral system that many Palestinians regard as discriminatory became a means of resisting the government responsible for policies they opposed.
Israel’s caste-like divide

The election also revealed another, less visible division within Jewish Israeli society. The Jewish population is broadly divided between Ashkenazi Jews, with origins in Europe, and Mizrahi Jews, whose roots are in West Asia and northern Africa. The categories overlap in some families and do not determine individual political views, but they have played an important role in Israeli politics.

For decades after Israel’s establishment in 1948, Ashkenazi Jews dominated the country’s political, military, academic, and economic institutions. Many Mizrahi immigrants, arriving from Morocco, Iraq, Yemen, and other countries, encountered poorer housing, limited opportunities, and discrimination.

The resulting resentments helped reshape Israeli politics. The Labour establishment, historically dominated by Ashkenazi elites, lost its monopoly over political power when Menachem Begin’s Likud won the 1977 election. Likud subsequently developed a durable base among Mizrahi and working-class voters. This produced a political paradox that remains visible today.
Netanyahu himself comes from an Ashkenazi family, like many prominent Likud leaders. Yet the party’s strongest and most loyal constituencies include substantial numbers of Mizrahi voters.

Natenyahu’s principal challenger, Eisenkot, belongs to a Moroccan Jewish family. Yet his Yashar! party draws support from constituencies associated with Israel’s more secular, liberal and economically established centre, including many Ashkenazi voters.

An Ashkenazi-led Likud continues to draw strength from Mizrahi resentment towards old elites, while a Mizrahi challenger seeks to replace Netanyahu with support from voters historically associated with those elites.

Were Eisenkot to become Prime Minister, he would be the first Israeli leader of Mizrahi family origin to hold the office. But his Moroccan ancestry does not mean that he shares the political demands of Palestinian citizens. Eisenkot represents an alternative to Netanyahu’s leadership rather than a fundamental rejection of Israel’s prevailing security doctrine.

A former military chief, he has opposed Palestinian statehood in the aftermath of the Hamas terror attack on October 7, 2023. His prospective coalition partners include politicians whose positions on Palestinian rights are often as restrictive as those of Netanyahu’s existing allies.

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett supports Israeli sovereignty over substantial areas of the occupied West Bank. Lieberman, a former Defence Minister, has long advocated hard-line security policies. Both previously served under Netanyahu. Both now oppose his continued leadership. Their political differences with him are real, but they should not be mistaken for agreement with Palestinian demands for sovereignty and self-determination.

For Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, the election raises a more disturbing possibility than the continuation of Netanyahu’s rule. Some observers fear that Netanyahu’s removal could weaken international pressure on Israel, even if the policies responsible for Palestinian suffering remain substantially unchanged.

A government headed by Eisenkot could present itself as a responsible alternative, promising to repair relations with Western governments, restore institutional discipline, and moderate some of the rhetoric associated with Netanyahu’s far-right Ministers. Such a change could be welcomed by European governments eager to restore diplomatic normality with Israel.

The Israeli human rights organisation B’Tselem argues that international pressure must not depend on which politician occupies the Prime Minister’s office. B’Tselem representatives Yuli Novak and Yair Dvir warned against treating Netanyahu as the sole architect of Palestinian dispossession.

“We are not seeing any possibility of change that will come from within the system,” Dvir said. Novak, the organisation’s executive director, placed the present crisis within a much longer history. “Settlement, ethnic cleansing, dehumanisation, military control, apartheid, these are all things that were there way, way before,” she said. She argued that Netanyahu’s departure would not automatically dismantle the institutions and policies through which Israel exercises control over Palestinian lives.

Jewish settlers living in the occupied West Bank can vote for Israel’s parliament. Palestinians living nearby, subject to Israeli military authority, generally cannot. Palestinians in Gaza also have no vote in Israeli parliamentary elections, despite the profound influence of Israeli military and political decisions over their lives. Most Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem possess residency rather than Israeli citizenship and likewise cannot participate in national elections.

The result is a political system in which millions of people live under varying degrees of Israeli control without enjoying an equal right to determine the government responsible for major decisions affecting their lives. The October 27 election has not resolved that contradiction.

It has, however, demonstrated the political strength that Palestinian citizens of Israel can exercise when they participate in large numbers. Their votes prevented Netanyahu from securing another parliamentary majority. Their representatives now hold seats that could influence the formation of the next government. Whether that influence produces changes in public policy remains uncertain.

The US midterm elections have added another layer of uncertainty. Netanyahu’s relationship with Trump, once presented as an assurance of political and diplomatic strength, has become a subject of controversy as the President faces a more assertive Congress. But Trump’s diminished political leverage does not by itself guarantee Netanyahu’s departure.

The immediate decision rests with Israel’s opposition leaders. They must determine whether their disagreements over Palestinian representation are more important than their shared objective of replacing Netanyahu.

The election has changed the arithmetic of Israeli politics. Whether it changes the lives of Palestinians will depend not only on who governs Israel but also on whether the world continues to demand accountability, whichever government takes office.

Netanyahu’s fate may have become entangled with the midterm elections in the US. But the political crisis that threatens his premiership began much closer to home, in Palestinian towns and villages where voters who had long remained outside electoral politics decided that this time their votes could make a difference. Now the question is whether Israel’s Jewish opposition is prepared to accept the consequences of that democratic verdict.
Iftikhar Gilani is an Indian journalist based in Ankara.
